sources.title: Pilatesology Encyclopedia: The Saw
facts: Keep the opposite hip on the mat during the reach.
Initiate the twist from the waist; reach the fingers toward the opposite little toe.
Maintain abdominal support in the forward curved position.

sources.title: Pilatesology Encyclopedia: The Spine Twist
facts: Sit upright rather than dropping behind the hips.
Keep the feet flexed and together.
Maintain a lifted spine during the twist.

sources.title: Pilatesology Encyclopedia: Criss-Cross
facts: Lift and twist the torso instead of moving the shoulders alone.
Keep the torso controlled rather than rocking during the leg change.
Maintain consistent leg length and height through the change.

sources.title: The Classical Pilates Mat Exercises Listed
sources.locator: The 34 exercises listed in Return to Life order
facts: The list places Saw at 11 and Spine Twist at 19.
Items 14 and 16 are Double Leg Kick and Scissors, respectively.
Criss-Cross does not appear in this original 34-exercise list. This list is used for numbering only, not pose geometry.

rotation-mat-saw.nameEn: The Saw (Seated Wide V-Sit Axial Rotation & Diagonal Reach)

sourceSupportedCues.rotationAxis: Turn the torso, then reach diagonally toward the opposite foot.
sourceSupportedCues.pelvisAnchor: Keep the opposite hip supported on the mat; reduce the reach if it lifts.
sourceSupportedCues.transitionPose: Return with control; the illustrated phase timings are authored.

rotation-mat-spine-twist.nameKo: 스파인 트위스트 (The Spine Twist · 장좌 수직 축 몸통 회전)
rotation-mat-spine-twist.nameEn: The Spine Twist (Long-Sitting Upright Seated Rotation)

sourceSupportedCues.rotationAxis: Twist while maintaining an upright, lifted seated torso.
sourceSupportedCues.pelvisAnchor: Keep feet together and flexed; avoid dropping behind the hips.
sourceSupportedCues.transitionPose: Return to center with control; the illustrated sequencing is authored.

rotation-mat-spine-twist.illustrationLimits: Joint angles, fixed anchors, gaze, apparent depth, phase timing and muscle overlays are authored simplifications, not individual anatomical targets or clinical measurements.
